source.title: Sharp Minima Can Generalize For Deep Nets
source.authors: Laurent Dinh; Razvan Pascanu; Samy Bengio; Yoshua Bengio

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied. No apparent truncation affecting the paper's main argument.
record.tranche_reason: The paper argues that common sharpness and flatness measures can be changed arbitrarily by reparameterizing rectified networks without changing the represented function or its generalization; it refines the proposed link between flatness and generalization.
record.gate_note: The paper's own findings are theoretical constructions and arguments, not empirical measurements of train/test error. It tests V7 by showing sharpness measures can fail to track generalization under equivalent parameterizations. Other versions are discussed or cited, not tested. Cited empirical findings are not rows.
record.test_reason: The paper proves parameterization dependence of several flatness measures, but does not test V7's magnitude-aware perturbation measure or its correlation and ranking of generalization gaps. Its theoretical results address a broader sharpness hypothesis outside the supplied versions. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's conclusion is accurate: commonly used flatness definitions require further context because symmetries and reparameterizations can alter loss geometry while preserving predictions and generalization. Flatness arguments must specify the model parameterization and input representation. This does not establish failure of V7's particular magnitude-aware empirical measure.
record.recipe_differences: The paper gives theoretical constructions and derivations about equivalent parameters and reparameterizations; it does not empirically compare trained checkpoints or measure generalization gaps.
record.method_sensitivity: Flatness conclusions depend on the parameterization and measure; the paper also distinguishes full-space from random-subspace epsilon-sharpness.

fits_no_version.finding: Rectifier scaling preserves the prediction function while volume flatness is infinite and Hessian curvature or full-space epsilon-sharpness can be large.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Several conventional flatness measures cannot universally rank generalization without accounting for parameter-space symmetries.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight normalization permits arbitrarily low full-space and random-subspace epsilon-sharpness with respect to its unnormalized parameter while preserving predictions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sharpness measured in weight-normalization coordinates can change independently of the represented function.

fits_no_version.finding: Model reparameterization can change curvature and the relative flatness of minima without changing their prediction functions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unqualified geometric explanations of generalization depend on the chosen parameterization.

record.problems: The findings bearing on V7 are theoretical rather than empirical; the paper does not measure train/test gaps across trained networks. The text notes that it has not been able to show the same problem for random-subspace epsilon-sharpness in the relevant discussion, while a later summary makes a broader claim about it.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Cited empirical claims about flat minima and generalization (including Keskar et al. 2017) were not extracted as this paper's results.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on random versus natural labels.
Held-out error as width increases beyond the width needed to fit training data.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizer versus SGD generalization under different tuning regimes.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and remedies through recipe changes.

Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps within a convolutional family, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures. The paper also does not directly test V7's cited empirical sharpness failures.
Test-accuracy effects of removing highly memorized versus random training examples.

record.verdict_notes: Theoretical arguments can qualify as tests, but these constructions concern different measures from the one V7 names. The record's V7 challenge label should therefore be removed. Its claimed inconsistency about random-subspace sharpness disappears when Section 4.3's rectifier scaling is distinguished from Section 5.1's weight-normalization scaling.

versions.untested_parts: Memorization of random labels and generalization on natural labels.
Test error across widths past the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected test error.
Generalization differences between adaptive optimizers and SGD.
Large-batch generalization gap and recipe adjustments.

No magnitude-aware sharpness measure or empirical ranking of generalization gaps; results concern volume flatness, Hessian trace/spectral norm, and epsilon-sharpness for rectified networks under equivalent transformations. No CIFAR-10/SVHN comparative experiment.
Removal of memorized examples and test-accuracy effects.

rows.subject: one-hidden layer rectified neural network
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical alpha-scale transformation produces observationally equivalent parameters with arbitrarily changed volume epsilon-flatness.
rows.value: infinite volume epsilon-flatness for every minimum, as stated by the theorem
rows.note: The theorem makes volume epsilon-flatness identical in its infinite value across minima; this measure cannot rank generalization.
rows.check: Volume flatness is not V7's magnitude-aware sharpness. Theorem 2 establishes infinite volume for each qualifying minimum, rather than an opposite generalization effect. The subject requires both weight matrices to be nonzero.

rows.subject: one-hidden layer rectified neural network
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical alpha-scale transformation of equivalent parameters changes Hessian spectral norm and trace without changing the represented function.
rows.measure: Hessian spectral norm and trace as sharpness measures
rows.value: an observationally equivalent minimum can have arbitrarily large spectral norm; the paper says the same conclusion applies to trace
rows.locator: Section 4.2, Theorem 4 and discussion following proof
rows.note: The paper states that if one minimum generalizes better than another, an equivalent parameter can be made sharper by spectral norm; thus this measure does not reliably track generalization.
rows.check: Unnormalized Hessian spectral norm and trace do not measure V7's magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance. Arbitrarily increasing curvature while preserving predictions does not establish a reversed correlation for that measure.

rows.subject: deep rectified feedforward network
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical layerwise rescaling of equivalent parameters raises many Hessian eigenvalues.
rows.measure: Number of Hessian eigenvalues that can be made arbitrarily large
rows.value: r − mink≤K(nk) eigenvalues can be made greater than any M > 0
rows.note: This is a theoretical result about Hessian eigenvalues under equivalent parameterizations, not an empirical correlation with test error.
rows.check: The eigenvalue construction does not test V7. The stated bound is at least r − min_k(n_k) eigenvalues above any M > 0; it gives a nontrivial count only when this difference is positive.

rows.subject: one-hidden layer rectified neural network
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical alpha-scale transformation changes full-space epsilon-sharpness while preserving predictions.
rows.value: an equivalent parameter can have high full-space epsilon-sharpness; the paper also states arbitrarily low full-space epsilon-sharpness is possible
rows.note: The full-space epsilon-sharpness can vary independently of the represented function; the paper says this weakens its link to generalization.
rows.check: The row combines different constructions. Section 4.3 uses rectifier alpha-scaling to obtain high full-space epsilon-sharpness. Section 5.1 obtains arbitrarily low sharpness through isotropic scaling of the unnormalized weight-normalization parameter v. Separate these conditions. Neither establishes a result for V7's measure.

rows.subject: one-hidden layer rectified neural network
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical alpha-scale transformation changes random-subspace epsilon-sharpness while preserving predictions.
rows.value: the Section 5 summary states an equivalent parameter can have arbitrarily low random-subspace epsilon-sharpness
rows.note: The paper explicitly says it has not shown the same problem for random-subspace sharpness in the preceding discussion; its later summary claims an equivalent parameter can have arbitrarily low random-subspace sharpness. This is a theoretical claim, not an empirical comparison.
rows.check: The subject and transformation are misattributed. Arbitrarily low random-subspace sharpness is stated in Section 5.1 for weight normalization, with respect to v under v → alpha v. Section 4.3's inability to establish an analogous rectifier alpha-scaling result concerns a different construction; these passages are not contradictory.

rows.subject: function f under a reparametrization
rows.operation_detail: A bijective reparametrization changes loss geometry while preserving the prediction function.
rows.value: sharp minima in one parameterization can correspond to flat minima in another, and conversely
rows.note: This is a general theoretical argument about parameterization dependence of flatness, not a measured test-error relationship.
rows.check: This is a valid theoretical result about curvature under model reparameterization, not a reversed result for V7's magnitude-aware measure. The Hessian derivation requires the relevant differentiability assumptions, beyond merely specifying a bijection.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Rectified networks under equivalent alpha-scale transformations; Hessian and epsilon-sharpness measures
reader_labels.reason: Equivalent parameters can have arbitrarily altered sharpness while representing the same function, challenging the claim that sharpness tracks the generalization gap (R1–R6).
